editor_note: Diligence gaps dominate: an inherited Russian contract cost Extreme Networks a sanctions penalty, a USPS bribery plea spotlights procurement risk, and the EEOC rolls back criminal-records guidance as Canada targets non-competes.

bottom_line.text: OFAC fined Extreme Networks $1.53M over Russian sales; test ownership screening and acquired customer books.
EEOC rescinded criminal-records guidance; review background-check policies against state fair-chance laws.
Ex-USPS procurement official pleads guilty to bribery; audit hospitality and intermediaries near government buyers.
Canada’s Competition Bureau wants non-competes limited; inventory clauses in Canadian contracts.

cards.title: Extreme Networks pays $1.53M after Russian unit sold to blocked missile maker
cards.summary: OFAC settled nine apparent Russia sanctions violations with Extreme Networks after its Russian subsidiary sold networking gear to a blocked air-defence manufacturer through an inherited contract, despite repeated end-user red flags.
cards.impact: Re-check ownership-based screening, end-user verification and acquired customer books; OFAC says written procedures fail when red flags in order data are ignored.

cards.title: EEOC votes to rescind enforcement guidance on arrest and conviction records
cards.summary: The EEOC voted to rescind its Title VII enforcement guidance on how employers consider arrest and conviction records in employment decisions.
cards.impact: Review background-check policies built on the guidance; state and local fair-chance laws still apply even as federal guidance is withdrawn.

cards.title: Smithfield Fresh Meats to pay $245,000 to settle EEOC pregnancy discrimination suit
cards.summary: Pork processor Smithfield Fresh Meats, with a plant in Tar Heel, North Carolina, will pay $245,000 and provide other relief to settle an EEOC pregnancy discrimination lawsuit.
cards.impact: Check pregnancy accommodation practices and supervisor training at plant level, where EEOC continues to bring PWFA and Title VII cases.

cards.title: Former USPS procurement official pleads guilty to bribery tied to contracts worth hundreds of millions
cards.summary: James E. Lee Sr., a former U.S. Postal Service procurement official, pleaded guilty to conspiring to commit bribery and honest services wire fraud related to large contracts.
cards.impact: Government contractors should verify gifts, hospitality and intermediary payments touching procurement officials; bribery pleas often lead to probes of the paying vendors.

cards.title: SEC charges two entities in $130 million fraud scheme built on false SEC filings
cards.summary: The SEC charged BG Wealth Sharing Ltd and DSJ Exchange Pty Ltd, foreign-operated Colorado-incorporated entities, with a $130 million fraud that used false SEC filings to boost investor confidence.
cards.impact: A reminder to verify counterparties beyond regulatory filings; a registration or filing is not proof of legitimacy in onboarding diligence.

cards.title: Labor Department finalizes pharmacy benefit manager fee transparency rule
cards.summary: DOL's Employee Benefits Security Administration finalized a rule requiring pharmacy benefit managers and affiliated brokers and consultants to disclose compensation to health plans.
cards.impact: Plan fiduciaries should prepare to collect and review PBM disclosures and document reasonableness reviews of their benefits vendors.

cards.title: DOJ unveils indictments in nationwide 'ghost student' fraud linked to Kenyan network
cards.summary: DOJ's new National Fraud Enforcement Division and three U.S. Attorney's offices announced indictments in a nationwide scheme using fake 'ghost students', linked to a Kenyan network.
cards.impact: Institutions handling federal funds should test identity verification controls; DOJ is staffing up dedicated fraud enforcement.

cards.title: Internal audit budgets rise, but cyber and AI risks outpace capacity
cards.summary: Survey roundup: internal audit budgets are rising but cyber and AI risks are outrunning the function; directors say strategy execution needs the most oversight improvement.
cards.impact: Use the findings to benchmark audit coverage of AI and cyber risk in the annual plan and board reporting.

cards.title: GRC business roundup: Casepoint, Smarsh, LexisNexis, EcoVadis and more
cards.summary: A roundup of product launches and business news from GRC technology vendors including Casepoint, Smarsh, LexisNexis and EcoVadis.
cards.impact: Useful market scan for anyone tracking GRC tooling and competitive moves in the compliance software space.

cards.title: Competition Bureau urges provinces and territories to limit non-compete clauses
cards.summary: Canada's Competition Bureau called on provinces and territories to limit the widespread use of non-competes, saying worker mobility drives competition, better pay and entrepreneurship.
cards.impact: Inventory non-competes in Canadian employment contracts; provincial restrictions (as in Ontario) may spread, making broad clauses unenforceable.

cards.title: Canada's privacy commissioners call for responsible AI use in health and health research
cards.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial privacy commissioners and ombuds issued a joint call for the responsible use of artificial intelligence in health care and health research.
cards.impact: Organizations using health data for AI should map consent, de-identification and accountability practices against regulators' joint expectations.

cards.title: Digital omnibus sparks EU lobbying frenzy
cards.summary: Euractiv's tech briefing covers intense lobbying around the EU digital omnibus, plus frontier AI, Frontex and IAB Europe.
cards.impact: The omnibus could reshape GDPR and AI Act obligations; keep compliance roadmaps flexible until the final text settles.

cards.summary: Meta has dropped its deadline for new AI business terms and will consult further with industry after objections from publishers.
cards.impact: Vendor terms on AI data use can change quickly; track supplier AI clauses and keep the right to object in contracts.

3d0904e53085.headline: Extreme Networks pays $1.53M after Russian unit sold to blocked missile maker
3d0904e53085.dek: An inherited Russian contract and ignored red flags led to OFAC and DOJ resolutions over sales to a blocked air-defence manufacturer.
3d0904e53085.body_md:
The U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced on October 27 that Extreme Networks, a North Carolina-based networking company, agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The Justice Department resolved a parallel investigation the same day through a non-prosecution agreement, and part of the OFAC amount is credited against the DOJ payment.

**What happened.** In March 2018, the company's Russian subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, bought customer accounts and contracts from another Russian networking business. One inherited contract named JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA) as end user. MMZA was majority-owned by Concern Almaz-Antey, designated by OFAC in 2014, so it was treated as blocked under the ownership rule. MMZA builds missiles for the S-300 and S-400 air defence systems and was designated in its own right in June 2022.

Between 2018 and early 2022, the subsidiary handled nine orders of routing switches, ports, power supplies, software and subscriptions for MMZA, while paperwork named a different Russian company as end user. According to OFAC, seven of the orders carried MMZA email addresses or its Moscow address, staff met MMZA personnel in person, and MMZA employees were told to register on the customer portal under the other company's name.

**Why the screening failed.** OFAC said the central compliance team reviewed the 2018 contract and screened all nine orders, yet missed the blocked ownership and did not follow up on red flags such as email domains, ship-to addresses and a shifting end-user explanation. The agency deemed the case egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed; the base penalty was $1,699,650, half the statutory maximum. Remediation, including stronger screening, end-user diligence, more compliance staff and better M&A diligence, counted in the company's favour. A law-firm analysis notes the settlement also requires a sanctions compliance programme with annual executive certification for five years.

### What compliance teams should do
- Screen ownership, not just names: apply the 50 Percent Rule, including indirect and aggregated holdings.
- Cross-check every data point on an order (email domains, addresses, signatures) against the declared end user, and treat a mismatch as a hold.
- In acquisitions, including asset and contract purchases, screen the full inherited customer book before continuing any relationship.
- Give foreign affiliates in high-risk markets direct oversight and route field intelligence to compliance; evaluate voluntary self-disclosure early.
